newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Congress gathers to settle re-election.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Congress gathers to settle re-election.

text.p: Brazilian deputies and senators were due to return to Congress this week to begin deciding the fate of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's dream of running for an unprecendented second consecutive term.
An extraordinary, month-long session of Congress began officially on Monday with a constitutional amendment to allow re-election the hottest item on a packed agenda.

Other items include bills to regulate the opening up of Brazil's oil and gas and telecommunications industries to the private sector while the Senate may begin to rewrite a social security reform that was rendered effectively useless by the Chamber of Deputies last year.
"January will be a decisive month," said analyst Carlos Setti of Goes e Consultores. "The fundamental questions for the next few years are in the home stretch in Congress."

Government leaders hope to put the re-election amendment to a vote in a Chamber of Deputies committee in the week beginning January 13, followed days later by a first of two votes on the floor of the lower house.
The amendment is expected to sail through the committee, where it requires only a simple majority, but faces a rough ride on the lower house floor where it needs two three-fifths majorities.
"Clearly, January is going to be a tense month," the government's leader in the upper house, Sen. Elcio Alvares, told newspaper Folha de Sao Paulo.

Rewriting the Constitution to allow re-election would undo one of the founding tenets of the Brazilian Republic, and the prospect of allowing Cardoso to benefit from the reform has brought congressional intrigue to the boil.

Government leaders say they already have more than enough support for approval of re-election in the lower house. But that claim is challenged by Paulo Maluf, the former mayor of Sao Paulo whose own presidential ambitions depend largely on defeating re-election.

"They won't vote to put the amendment on the voting agenda because they don't have enough votes for its approval. If they do, they'll be defeated," Maluf told newspaper Jornal do Brasil from hospital, where he is recovering from an operation to remove a malignant tumor from his prostrate gland.

Maluf's machinations are the not the only worry for the government. The Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB) and the Liberal Front Party (PFL), the two biggest parties in Congress whose votes are crucial to the re-election push, are at loggerheads over upcoming elections for the presidencies of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.

Normally the two parties agree to run one house each, but the PMBD's insistence on fielding candidates for both houses has incensed the PFL and threatens a destabilising rift that could undo the government's calculations of support for re-election.
"The government could vote on re-election, but that would not be recommended without an agreement (between the PMBD and PFL)," said analyst Setti.
